IAF

Who leads the IAF right now

  • Chief of the Air Staff: ACM Amar Preet Singh, since 30 Sep 2024. He retires on 31 Oct 2026.
  • Next Chief: Air Marshal Ashutosh Dixit, the current Vice Chief, was named on 6 Oct 2026 and takes over on 31 Oct 2026 as the 29th Chief of the Air Staff, with a tenure reported to run to 31 Dec 2028.
  • Chief of Defence Staff: Gen N.S. Raja Subramani, since 31 May 2026.
  • Motto: Nabhah Sparsham Deeptam, "Touch the sky with glory".

History · 1925 to 2026

From Wapitis
to Rafales

19322026

How a single flight of four biplanes at Karachi became the world's fourth-largest air force: the founding, the wars, the chiefs and the people the IAF still talks about.

As of 17 October 2026

1925 to 1945

Birth and the war years

Skeen Committee to the Royal prefix

  1. 1925

    The Skeen (Indian Sandhurst) Committee is set up. Its 1927 report recommends an air arm and training for Indian officers at RAF College Cranwell.

  2. 1930

    Six Indians enter Cranwell, among them Subroto Mukerjee. J.N. Tandon later becomes the first equipment (logistics) officer.

  3. 19 Jan 1932

    The first airmen are recruited. They are kitted like sepoys and called Havai Sepoys.

  4. 8 Apr 1932

    The Indian Air Force Act receives the Governor General's assent.

  5. 8 Oct 1932

    The IAF is established when the Act is notified in the Gazette, as an auxiliary of the RAF. 8 October becomes Air Force Day.

  6. 1 Apr 1933

    'A' Flight of No. 1 Squadron forms at Drigh Road, Karachi, with four Westland Wapiti biplanes, six RAF-trained officers and 19 Havai Sepoys.

  7. 1936 to 1939

    'B' and 'C' Flights are added. Six Coastal Defence Flights guard the coast from Karachi to Calcutta with Wapitis and Atalantas.

  8. 1943 to 1945

    The Burma campaign is the IAF's first real war: reconnaissance, close support and bombing against the Japanese. The force grows to nine squadrons by 1945.

  9. 12 Mar 1945

    King George VI grants the prefix 'Royal' for wartime service. The force becomes the Royal Indian Air Force.

IAF

Remember

  • Founded: 8 October 1932, as an auxiliary of the RAF.
  • First unit: 'A' Flight, No. 1 Squadron, 1 April 1933, Drigh Road, Karachi.
  • First aircraft: Westland Wapiti, a British biplane.
  • First combat: the North-West Frontier, then Burma in 1943 to 1945.
  • Royal: granted 12 March 1945, dropped 26 January 1950.

1947 to 2026

Independent India's air force

Partition to the present

  1. 1947

    Partition splits the force: two squadrons go to Pakistan and India keeps the rest. No. 12 Squadron's Dakotas evacuate about 30,000 refugees.

  2. 27 Oct 1947

    Dakotas fly the 1st Sikh into Srinagar and save the Valley. The J&K war runs to 1 January 1949.

  3. 1949

    Operational and Training Commands form. Maintenance Command follows in 1955.

  4. 26 Jan 1950

    India becomes a Republic. 'Royal' is dropped, and the tricolour roundel replaces the British one.

  5. 1 Apr 1954

    Air Marshal Subroto Mukerjee becomes the first Indian Commander-in-Chief of the IAF.

  6. 1950s

    The jet age: Vampires, Toofanis, Mysteres, Hunters, Canberras and Gnats join the fleet.

  7. 1960 to 1961

    Canberras fly for the United Nations in the Congo.

  8. Dec 1961

    Operation Vijay: Goa is liberated in 36 hours, the first joint operation of the three services.

  9. 1962

    War with China. Transport and helicopter crews supply the front, but offensive air power is held back.

  10. 1963

    The MiG-21 arrives, the start of a 62-year career.

  11. 1965

    War with Pakistan. Gnats earn the name 'Sabre Slayer'.

  12. 1971

    The Bangladesh war. The IAF wins air superiority over East Pakistan in days, drops paratroopers at Tangail and bombs the Governor's House in Dhaka. Fg Offr N.J.S. Sekhon wins the Param Vir Chakra.

  13. 3 Apr 1984

    Sqn Ldr Rakesh Sharma becomes the first Indian in space.

  14. 13 Apr 1984

    Operation Meghdoot: IAF helicopters and transports start sustaining troops on the Siachen Glacier, which they still do.

  15. 1987 to 1990

    Operation Pawan in Sri Lanka: about 70,000 transport and helicopter sorties without losing an aircraft.

  16. 3 Nov 1988

    Operation Cactus: IL-76s fly paratroopers over 2,000 km from Agra to the Maldives and stop a coup within hours.

  17. 1999

    Kargil, Operation Safed Sagar: about 1,200 fighter and 2,500 helicopter sorties at altitudes above 15,000 ft.

  18. 2002

    Arjan Singh is made Marshal of the Indian Air Force.

  19. 2004

    The Garud Commando Force is raised.

  20. 2013

    Operation Rahat in Uttarakhand: about 19,600 people airlifted, the largest helicopter rescue by any air force.

  21. 2016

    The first three women fighter pilots are commissioned, and the first Tejas squadron forms.

  22. 26 Feb 2019

    Balakot: Mirage 2000s strike a Jaish-e-Mohammed camp in Pakistan.

  23. 2020

    Rafales arrive at Ambala. The IAF airlifts forces to Ladakh during the stand-off with China.

  24. 2022

    The Weapon Systems Branch is approved, the first new branch since Independence.

  25. May 2025

    Operation Sindoor after the Pahalgam attack: strikes on terror camps, then on Pakistani air bases.

  26. 26 Sep 2025

    The MiG-21 is retired at Chandigarh.

  27. 2026

    HTT-40 trainers begin delivery, Tarang Shakti 2026 is held at Jodhpur, and a new Chief takes over on 31 October.

Sources

  • IAF: history
  • Bharat Rakshak: IAF history
  • PIB: MiG-21 farewell

Heroes

Names worth knowing

Pioneers, gallantry and space

Subroto Mukerjee

Air Marshal · first Indian chief

One of the first six Indians trained at RAF Cranwell. Took command of No. 1 Squadron as the first Indian commanding officer, and in 1954 became the first Indian to head the IAF. Remembered as the father of the IAF.

K.K. 'Jumbo' Majumdar

Squadron Leader · WWII

Turned the Lysander, a reconnaissance aircraft, into a bomber against Japanese air bases in Burma. First IAF officer to win the Distinguished Flying Cross, and later the first to win a bar to it, flying with an RAF squadron in Europe.

Mehar Singh, MVC

Air Commodore · 1947 to 48

Led air operations in J&K. Landed the first Dakota on a 600-yard strip at Poonch, and on 24 May 1948 flew Maj Gen K.S. Thimayya to Leh in an unpressurised Dakota over mountains up to 24,000 ft. Awarded the Maha Vir Chakra.

Arjan Singh, DFC

Marshal of the IAF

Led a squadron in Burma in 1944 and the IAF through the 1965 war as Chief of the Air Staff. Made Marshal of the Indian Air Force in 2002, the only five-star rank the IAF has had. Died in 2017.

Nirmal Jit Singh Sekhon, PVC

Flying Officer · 1971

On 14 Dec 1971 he took off in a Gnat from Srinagar while six PAF Sabres were bombing the airfield, fought them alone, hit two and was shot down. The IAF's first and only Param Vir Chakra, awarded posthumously.

Rakesh Sharma, AC

Squadron Leader · 1984

IAF fighter pilot who flew on Soyuz T-11 on 3 April 1984 and became the first Indian in space. Awarded the Ashoka Chakra and Hero of the Soviet Union. His reply from orbit, "Saare Jahan Se Achha", is part of IAF folklore.

Shubhanshu Shukla, AC

Group Captain · 2025

IAF test pilot and Gaganyaan astronaut-designate who flew to the International Space Station on Axiom-4 in June and July 2025, the first Indian aboard the ISS. Awarded the Ashoka Chakra on Republic Day 2026.

Jyoti Prakash Nirala, AC

Corporal · Garud

Garud commando killed while taking on terrorists at Bandipora, J&K, in November 2017. Awarded the Ashoka Chakra posthumously, the IAF's highest peacetime gallantry award for an airman.

Identity and honours

Symbols and
Gallantry

MottoMedals

The marks the IAF wears and flies, the days it keeps, and the awards its people have won, including the honours for Operation Sindoor.

As of 17 October 2026

Symbols

What the IAF flies under

Roundel, fin flash, ensign, crest, motto

Motto

  • Nabhah Sparsham Deeptam: "Touch the sky with glory". From the Bhagavad Gita, Chapter 11, verse 24, where Arjuna describes the cosmic form of Krishna touching the sky.

Crest

  • The State Emblem (Ashoka lion capital with Satyamev Jayate) on top; below it a Himalayan eagle with wings spread, inside a light blue ring reading Bharatiya Vayu Sena; the motto in golden Devanagari at the base.

Colours

  • Air Force blue uniforms; light blue rank braid on dark blue shoulder boards (see Organisation).

8 Oct

Air Force Day and traditions

The IAF's anniversary

Air Force Day

  • Held every 8 October, marking the 1932 founding. The parade was at Hindan for decades, moved to Chandigarh (2022), Prayagraj (2023) and Chennai (2024), and returned to Hindan in 2025 and 2026, with the big flypast held separately (Guwahati in Nov 2025, Varanasi on 25 Oct 2026).
  • 94th Air Force Day, 8 Oct 2026: theme 'Infallible, Impervious and Precise'. Parade at AFS Hindan reviewed by ACM A.P. Singh, with three Mi-17 1V helicopters in 'Dhwaj' formation carrying the national and IAF flags.

Traditions

  • IAF-1: a vintage Ford saloon that carried Air Chiefs for 23 years, used again at the 2026 parade.
  • Number-plating: when a squadron's aircraft retire, the squadron is 'number-plated' (stood down) and its number can later be revived with new aircraft.
  • Squadron names and crests: every squadron has a nickname, such as No. 17 'Golden Arrows' or No. 23 'Panthers', and its own crest and motto.

2025

Honours for Operation Sindoor

Announced 14 Aug 2025, Independence Day

IAF

Nine Vir Chakras

  • Nine Vir Chakras to IAF officers, out of 15 across the services: Gp Capt Ranjeet Singh Sidhu, Gp Capt Manish Arora, Gp Capt Animesh Patni, Gp Capt Kunal Kalra, Wg Cdr Joy Chandra, Sqn Ldr Sarthak Kumar, Sqn Ldr Siddhant Singh, Sqn Ldr Rizwan Malik and Flt Lt Aarshveer Singh Thakur.
  • Sarvottam Yudh Seva Medals: four of the seven awarded went to IAF Air Marshals: N. Tiwari, A.K. Bharti (then Director General Air Operations), Jeetendra Mishra and Nagesh Kapoor. The last IAF officer to get one was Air Marshal Vinod Patney, for Kargil.
  • Also: a Shaurya Chakra, 26 Vayu Sena Medals (Gallantry) and 13 Yudh Seva Medals to IAF personnel.

Primary role

  • Air defence of the country, and support to the Army and Navy, including airlift to places that roads cannot reach.

Secondary

  • In peace: stay ready for war, aid the civil power, and bring relief in disasters at home and abroad.

CDS

  • The Chief of Defence Staff, Gen N.S. Raja Subramani since 31 May 2026, heads the Department of Military Affairs and is the government's principal military adviser. He does not command the services' operations.

The seven commands

Five operational, two functional

CommandHQRoleAOC-in-CSince

Inside a command

  • Each command is led by an Air Officer Commanding-in-Chief (AOC-in-C), an Air Marshal.
  • Operational and Training Commands have three branches: the Senior Air Staff Officer (SASO) for operations, the Senior Officer-in-Charge Administration (SOA) and the Senior Maintenance Staff Officer (SMSO).
  • Maintenance Command combines air and admin under the SAASO, and adds an Air Officer-in-Charge Logistics Management (AOLM).

Also

  • The Andaman and Nicobar Command at Port Blair is a tri-service command. The IAF's Car Nicobar base works under it.

Station

Inside an air force station

Wing, station and lodger units

Station

  • A Wing or Station is self-accounting: it runs its own administration. A squadron is a lodger unit that depends on its station, so that it can concentrate on flying.
  • The station commander has three main heads: the Chief Operations Officer (flying, air traffic control, met, navigation and weapons), the Chief Engineering Officer (servicing, signals, armament, refuelling) and the Chief Administrative Officer (security, works, messing, welfare, education and civilians).
  • Medical and accounts sections report directly to the station commander.

Squadron

  • The basic fighting unit. A fighter squadron has about 16 to 18 aircraft, led by a Wing Commander (commanding officer).
  • Squadrons are split into flights led by Squadron Leaders.
  • FBSU: a Forward Base Support Unit runs a forward airfield that has no permanent squadron.

Ranks

Officer ranks and insignia

Light blue braid on dark blue shoulder boards

Officers wear rank in light blue braid: 9/16 inch braid, 1/4 inch braid and a 2 inch band for air officers. Air officers also wear stars on gorget (collar) patches: one for an Air Commodore up to five for the Marshal of the IAF. New officers are commissioned as Flying Officers; the old Pilot Officer rank is no longer used.

Airmen

Airmen and warrant ranks

Sleeve and shoulder badges

Airmen wear the eagle and chevrons on the sleeve; warrant ranks wear the State Emblem badge on the shoulder. Since 2022 airmen join as Agniveervayu under the Agnipath scheme for four years, and up to a quarter can be retained as regular airmen. JWO, WO and MWO are the IAF's warrant ranks, equal to the Army's JCOs.

ITC

The theatre command debate

Joint commands proposed since 2019

Idea

  • Integrated theatre commands would put Army, Navy and Air Force units in a region under one commander, as in the US and China.

IAF view

  • Air power is scarce, at 29 fighter squadrons, and works best when Air HQ can switch it between fronts within hours.
  • Splitting squadrons across theatres would lock them in place and dilute concentration of force.
  • Air assets should be commanded by airmen who know air doctrine.

Status

  • A proposal was submitted in April 2026 and awaits approval from the Defence Minister and the Cabinet Committee on Security. No theatre command had been created as of mid-October 2026.

Branches, entry and training

Branches
and Roles

BranchWings

Who does what in the IAF, how officers and airmen get in, and how a cadet becomes a front-line pilot.

As of 17 October 2026

3 + 1

Officer branches and their duties

Flying, Ground Duty (Technical and Non-Technical), Weapon Systems

BranchStreamWhat its officers do
FlyingFighter, transport, helicopter pilotsFly and fight. Fighter pilots train for air defence, strike and reconnaissance; transport pilots for airlift, air drops and casualty evacuation; helicopter pilots for assault, rescue and supply to posts like Siachen.
Weapon Systems (WS)Since 2022Operate surface-to-air missiles (S-400, MR-SAM, Akash), surface-to-surface missiles, remotely piloted aircraft (Heron, MQ-9B) and the weapon systems seats in twin-seat and multi-crew aircraft. First new operational branch since Independence.
Technical: AE(M)Aeronautical Engineering (Mechanical)Keep airframes, engines, hydraulics, landing gear, fuel systems and armament serviceable, and certify aircraft fit to fly.
Technical: AE(L)Aeronautical Engineering (Electronics)Look after avionics, radar, communications, navigation, electronic warfare and weapon electronics, in the air and on the ground.
AdministrationIncl. ATC and Fighter ControllerRun stations and personnel matters. Air Traffic Controllers manage take-offs, landings and airspace. Fighter Controllers use radar and AWACS pictures to guide fighters onto threats.
LogisticsSupply everything from fuel and spares to rations and clothing, through the IAF's online material management system.
AccountsManage budgets, pay, audit and public funds.
EducationTeach and design training, run promotion exams and education programmes.
MeteorologyForecast weather for flying and operations, from runway visibility to cyclone and dust-storm warnings.

Doctors, dentists and nurses serve with the IAF through the Armed Forces Medical Services. Navigator intake has stopped; the Weapon Systems Branch now provides weapon systems officers for multi-crew aircraft.

Entry

How officers and airmen join

Written exam, then a five-day Air Force Selection Board

RouteWhoForRun by
NDAAfter Class 12 with Physics and MathsFlying Branch (permanent commission); cadets train three years at NDA Khadakwasla, then at AFAUPSC exam, then SSB at an Air Force Selection Board
CDSE (AFA course)Graduates with Physics and Maths in Class 12Flying BranchUPSC exam, then AFSB
AFCATGraduates and engineersFlying (short service), Ground Duty Technical and Non-Technical, including MeteorologyIAF online exam, twice a year, then AFSB
NCC Special EntryNCC Air Wing 'C' certificate holdersFlying BranchThrough AFCAT notification, no written exam, then AFSB
AgniveervayuClass 12 or diploma; age 17.5 to 21Airmen, four-year engagement; up to 25% retainedAgnipath scheme since 2022

AFSB

  • Air Force Selection Boards at Dehradun, Mysuru, Gandhinagar and Varanasi test candidates over five days: screening, psychology tests, group tasks and an interview, then a conference.
  • Flying Branch candidates who are recommended also take the Computerised Pilot Selection System (CPSS), a pilot aptitude test widely treated as once in a lifetime.

Women

  • Women have flown fighters since 2016: Avani Chaturvedi, Bhawana Kanth and Mohana Singh were the first three.
  • Women fighter pilots were made a permanent scheme in February 2022. Women serve in every branch, including Weapon Systems; the first women's NDA batch passed out on 30 May 2025.

AFA

From cadet to front line

Air Force Academy, Dundigal, near Hyderabad

AFA

  • The Air Force Academy, Dundigal trains every officer cadet of every branch before commissioning. Raised in 1969 to 70 and formally inaugurated on 16 Jan 1971. Motto: Shram Se Siddhi, "achievement through diligence". Combined Graduation Parades are held each June and December.
  • Training lasts 62 weeks for Flying and Ground Duty (Technical) cadets and 52 weeks for Ground Duty (Non-Technical) cadets (AFCAT 2/2025).
  • Cadets are commissioned as Flying Officers and receive their 'wings' or branch badges at the parade.

Airmen

  • Airmen begin with joint basic training at the Airmen Training School, Belagavi, then go to trade training institutes at Tambaram, Jalahalli, Avadi and others.
  • Airmen trades are grouped into Group X (technical) and Group Y (non-technical and some technical).
StageWhereAircraftFor
Stage I (basic)Air Force Academy, DundigalPilatus PC-7 Mk II; HTT-40 joining from 2026All pilot cadets
Stage II (intermediate)Fighter: Air Force Station Hakimpet and others · Transport: Yelahanka · Helicopter: HakimpetKiran Mk I/II (fighter), Dornier 228 (transport), Chetak/ALH (helicopter)Streamed after Stage I
Stage III (advanced)Bidar and KalaikundaBAE Hawk Mk132Fighter pilots, before conversion to front-line types
IAF

Stage III and beyond

  • After Stage III on the Hawk, fighter pilots convert to their front-line type at an operational conversion unit or squadron.
  • The HTT-40, an HAL-built basic trainer, began deliveries on 18 Sep 2026. 70 are on order to reinforce the PC-7 fleet.
  • The Kiran is being phased out; a long-delayed Sitara intermediate jet trainer has not entered service.

Special units

Special
Units

GarudSurya Kiran

The commandos, display teams, test pilots and specialist units that sit outside the normal squadron structure.

As of 17 October 2026

8

Units to know

Special forces, display, test and VVIP

Garud Commando Force

Special forces · raised 6 Feb 2004

Authorised in September 2003 after attacks on air bases, and formally raised on 6 Feb 2004. Motto: Prahaar Se Suraksha, "security through striking". Roles: protecting air bases, combat search and rescue behind enemy lines, seizing airfields, special reconnaissance and counter-terrorism. Trains at the Garud Regimental Training Centre at Chandinagar, near Hindan. Garuds have served in J&K counter-terror operations and with the UN in Congo.

Surya Kiran Aerobatic Team

Display team · formed 1996

Based at Air Force Station Bidar under Training Command. Flew the Kiran Mk II until 2011 and was re-formed in February 2015 on the BAE Hawk Mk132. Flies nine jets in tight formation, one of very few nine-aircraft jet teams in the world.

Sarang Helicopter Display Team

Display team · formed Oct 2003

The IAF's helicopter display team, at Sulur since 2009. Flies five HAL Dhruv ALH helicopters in display colours since 2023. 'Sarang' means peacock in Sanskrit.

Akashganga

Skydiving team · formed 10 Aug 1987

The IAF skydiving team, based at Agra. Jumps from transport aircraft at Air Force Day and Republic Day events.

ASTE

Flight test · Bengaluru

The Aircraft and Systems Testing Establishment tests new aircraft and weapons and runs the IAF Test Pilots School. Air Marshal Ashutosh Dixit, the next Chief, is an experimental test pilot, as is astronaut Gp Capt Shubhanshu Shukla.

Paratrooper Training School

Airborne · Agra

Trains parachutists of all three services. Agra is also home to the IL-76, IL-78 and A-50 fleets and was the launch base for Operation Cactus in 1988.

Communication Squadron

VVIP flight · Palam

Flies the President, Vice President and Prime Minister. Its aircraft include two Boeing 777-300ER 'Air India One' jets with self-protection suites, Boeing Business Jets and Embraer executive jets.

TACDE

Tactics school · Gwalior

The Tactics and Air Combat Development Establishment trains fighter pilots in advanced air combat tactics. The IAF's equivalent of a 'Top Gun' school.

9 types
  • MBDA MeteorBeyond-visual-range air-to-air missileIn serviceOver 100 km+
    Type
    Beyond-visual-range air-to-air missile
    Origin
    European consortium / MBDA
    Range
    Over 100 km (reported)
    Guidance
    Inertial with datalink mid-course; active radar terminal
    Carried by / used by
    Rafale
    In service since
    2020
    • Ramjet-powered, so it keeps energy late in flight and has a large no-escape zone.

← PreviousAircraftNext →How it works

How it works · flight, radar, aircraft

How It
Works

LiftRadar

The basic physics and machinery behind everything else on this site, with simple diagrams.

As of 17 October 2026

4

Four forces of flight

Lift, weight, thrust, drag

Lift

  • Upward force made by the wings as air flows over them. It must equal weight for level flight.

Weight

  • Gravity acting on the aircraft's mass, fuel and load.

Thrust

  • Forward force from a jet engine or propeller. A jet's afterburner adds fuel into the exhaust for extra thrust.

Drag

  • Air resistance against motion. Designers shape aircraft to reduce it.

Lift

How a wing makes lift

Bernoulli and Newton describe the same thing

Bernoulli

  • Faster-moving air has lower pressure. The pressure difference across the wing gives lift. Same idea: a storm wind lifting a roof, or the venturi in a carburettor.

Newton

  • The wing, set at an angle of attack, deflects air downward; the air pushes the wing up (third law). Both explanations are correct views of the same airflow.

Controls

  • Ailerons on the wingtips roll the aircraft; elevators on the tailplane pitch it; the rudder on the fin yaws it.
  • Flaps on the trailing edge add lift and drag for take-off and landing.

Rotor

How a helicopter flies

Rotating wings, torque and the tail rotor

  • The main rotor blades are wings that spin. Tilting the rotor disc tilts the lift, moving the helicopter forwards, backwards or sideways.
  • Turning the rotor makes the body want to turn the other way (Newton's third law). The tail rotor pushes sideways to cancel this torque and gives yaw control.

6

Basic flight instruments

The 'six-pack'

InstrumentShows
Airspeed indicatorSpeed through the air, in knots (1 knot = 1.852 km/h)
Attitude indicator (artificial horizon)Pitch and bank against the horizon
AltimeterHeight above mean sea level, from air pressure
Turn coordinatorRate of turn and whether the turn is balanced (slip or skid)
Heading indicatorDirection the nose points
Vertical speed indicatorRate of climb or descent, in feet per minute

Mach

  • Mach number is speed divided by the local speed of sound. Mach 1 is about 1,225 km/h at sea level and less at altitude.

Fly-by-wire

  • Pilot inputs go to computers, which move the control surfaces. This lets unstable, very agile designs like the Tejas and Rafale fly safely.

Where jets fly

  • Jets cruise high, near the top of the troposphere and into the lower stratosphere, above most weather and where thin air means less drag.

Radar

Radar and electronic warfare

Radio Detection And Ranging

Principle

  • A radar sends radio pulses and times the echo. Range is the speed of light times the round-trip time, divided by two.

Primary vs secondary

  • Primary radar sees the reflection from any aircraft, friendly or not.
  • Secondary radar (SSR/IFF) asks the aircraft's transponder to reply with its identity and altitude. Hostile aircraft do not answer.

AESA

  • An Active Electronically Scanned Array uses hundreds of small transmit-receive modules to steer the beam electronically, with no moving dish. The Rafale's RBE2 and the Tejas Mk1A's radar are AESAs.

Self-protection

  • RWR (radar warning receiver): warns the pilot that a radar is tracking the aircraft.
  • MAWS (missile approach warning system): detects a missile's rocket motor and triggers countermeasures.
  • Chaff (clouds of metal-coated strips) confuses radar-guided missiles; flares (hot magnesium decoys) confuse heat-seekers.

Network

  • The IACCS joins ground radars, AWACS, aerostats and missile units into one national air picture for the IAF.

1 vs 2

Single-engine and twin-engine fighters

Why the IAF flies both

Single engineTwin engine
IAF examplesTejas Mk1 and Mk1A, Mirage 2000, Tejas Mk2 (coming); earlier the MiG-21 and MiG-27Rafale, Su-30MKI, MiG-29, Jaguar; AMCA (coming)
Engine-outIf the engine fails, the pilot must glide back or ejectCan usually fly home on the remaining engine; safer over mountains and the sea
Thrust and loadLess total thrust, so less fuel and weaponsMore thrust: heavier loads, longer range, better climb at high-altitude bases like Leh
Size and costSmaller, lighter, cheaper to buy and run; fewer engines to maintainLarger and costlier per hour; two engines to service
Radar signatureSmaller airframe, smaller radar returnBigger airframe, but room for larger radar and more sensors
Typical roleLight fighter in numbers: air defence, close supportHeavy multirole: air superiority, deep strike, long range

Why both

  • Air forces mix them to balance cost and capability: many affordable light fighters for numbers, plus fewer heavy twins for reach and punch.
  • The IAF's plan follows that pattern: Tejas Mk1A in large numbers alongside Rafale and Su-30MKI.

Asymmetric thrust

  • In a twin with widely spaced engines, losing one pushes the nose towards the dead engine. The pilot holds it straight with rudder. Fighters with engines close together, like the Rafale, feel this much less than propeller transports such as the C-295.

Thrust vectoring

  • The Su-30MKI's twin engines have nozzles that swivel, letting it point its nose in ways other fighters cannot at low speed.

1947–48

First Indo-Pakistani War

Kashmir Valley, Poonch, Ladakh

OutcomeCeasefire line drawn. India keeps the Valley, Jammu and Ladakh.

Cause

  • Partition in August 1947 left Jammu and Kashmir (J&K) undecided. Maharaja Hari Singh wanted independence, signed a standstill agreement with Pakistan and delayed accession to India.
  • Pakistan imposed an economic blockade, then invaded in October 1947 using Pashtun tribal militias (Lashkars).
  • Aim: take Srinagar and force the state's accession to Pakistan.
  • The invaders took Muzaffarabad, sacked Baramulla and cut the Mahura power station, which left Srinagar dark and in panic.
  • 26 Oct 1947: Hari Singh signed the Instrument of Accession. J&K became part of India and Indian intervention became legal.

Course

  • Terrain ran from the temperate Kashmir Valley to the high-altitude deserts of Ladakh.
  • The 1st Sikh Regiment was airlifted into the unpaved Srinagar airfield with the invaders only miles away.
  • Shalateng, 7 Nov 1947: armoured cars and infantry routed the tribal forces and secured Srinagar.
  • Uri: Brigadier Rajinder Singh's delaying action bought time for the Indian build-up in the Valley.
  • 1948 summer offensives: the siege of Poonch was lifted, Barwali Ridge captured, and Rajauri and Jhangar secured.
  • Zojila: General K.S. Thimayya authorised moving M3 Stuart light tanks up to 11,500 ft. The sudden armour broke the Pakistani defences and kept Ladakh and Leh in Indian hands.

Aftermath

  • India took the dispute to the United Nations as the war settled into attrition.
  • Ceasefire from 1 Jan 1949. The Karachi Agreement (July 1949) fixed a Ceasefire Line under UNCIP supervision.
  • India held the Kashmir Valley, Jammu and Ladakh. Pakistan held Gilgit-Baltistan and a western strip it calls “Azad Kashmir”.
IAF

The airlift that held Srinagar

LiftStrike
  • Without the IAF, ground forces could not have moved or been sustained in J&K's remote theatres.
  • Srinagar Airlift, 27 Oct 1947: C-47 Dakotas flew from Safdarjung carrying troops, ammunition and equipment into the Valley. This is credited with preventing the fall of the capital.
  • Close air support: Spitfires, Tempests and Harvards backed the ground troops.
  • Shalateng: strafing runs cut the lashkars' fighting strength and caused panic.
  • Sustaining garrisons: air drops to besieged Poonch and flights into the unpaved Leh strip kept a forward presence through the Himalayan winter.

Aircraft and weapons used

  • C-47 Dakota
  • Spitfire
  • Tempest
  • Harvard

1948

Operation Polo

Hyderabad

OutcomeHyderabad joins the Indian Union within five days.

Cause

  • The Nizam of Hyderabad ruled a large, landlocked, Hindu-majority state and refused to join the Indian Union.
  • He allowed the Razakars, a militant militia, to terrorise the population and suppress pro-integration movements.
  • India's concern: a hostile independent state in the middle of the peninsula threatened the balkanisation of southern India.

Course

  • 13 Sept 1948: Operation Polo began, a multi-pronged armour and infantry advance.
  • The Nizam's regular forces and the Razakars were dismantled within five days.

Aftermath

  • Hyderabad was formally incorporated into the Union by 18 Sept 1948.
  • Officially described as a “police action” that secured internal stability.
IAF

Strafing and airfield control

Strike
  • For both integration campaigns (Polo and Goa) the IAF was indispensable: it sped the enemy's collapse and kept ground casualties down.
  • Tempests made tactical and psychological strafing runs on retreating Razakar forces.
  • The IAF secured the Hakimpet and Begumpet airfields. That shut off airborne resupply or evacuation of the Nizam's army by outside sympathisers.

Aircraft and weapons used

  • Tempest

1961

Operation Vijay (Goa)

Goa, Daman and Diu

OutcomePortuguese forces surrender after 36 hours.

Cause

  • Portugal's authoritarian regime refused to give up Goa, Daman and Diu, treating them as overseas provinces, despite years of Indian diplomacy.
  • Triggers: continuing Portuguese provocations and the suppression of Goan freedom fighters.

Course

  • Launched December 1961 as a tri-service operation.
  • Over 30,000 Indian troops, with a naval blockade and air cover, faced about 3,300 Portuguese defenders.
  • The defenders lacked heavy weapons and resisted weakly.

Aftermath

  • The operation ended within 36 hours. Portuguese forces surrendered on 19 Dec 1961.
  • It ended European colonial rule on the subcontinent.
IAF

Air superiority and interdiction

Strike
  • Canberra bombers made precision strikes on the Dabolim runway, to stop Portuguese transport aircraft escaping and airborne reinforcements arriving.
  • Vampires and Mysteres hit communication nodes with rockets and cannon fire, notably the Bambolim wireless station.
  • Result: Portuguese command and control was paralysed and the garrisons were cut off from Lisbon, which hastened surrender.

Aircraft and weapons used

  • Canberra
  • Vampire
  • Mystere

1962

Sino-Indian War

NEFA in the east, Ladakh and Aksai Chin in the west

OutcomeChina keeps Aksai Chin and declares a ceasefire. No treaty.

Cause

  • Borders in the high Himalayas were undemarcated. India recognised the McMahon Line in the east (NEFA, now Arunachal Pradesh) and the Johnson Line in the west (Aksai Chin). China rejected both as British imperial legacies.
  • The 1959 Tibetan uprising and the Dalai Lama's asylum in India led Beijing to see an Indian attempt to undermine Chinese rule in Tibet.
  • Forward Policy (Nehru): small, isolated, poorly supplied outposts behind Chinese lines, meant to cut their logistics and assert Indian administration. China saw a threat to its Xinjiang-Tibet highway through Aksai Chin.
  • Indian failure: a major intelligence failure and strategic hubris. Leaders assumed China would not invade at scale and that skirmishes could be handled diplomatically.

Course

  • 20 Oct 1962: the PLA attacked in the east and west at once.
  • PLA advantages: Korean War veterans, acclimatised to altitude, stronger logistics, automatic weapons and heavy artillery.
  • East: the PLA forded the Namka Chu at night, got behind Indian strong points and destroyed under-equipped Rajput battalions. Indian troops lacked winter clothing and ammunition, and phone lines were cut. Retreat from Tawang, Se La and Bomdila followed.
  • Walong: accurate mortar fire held the advance for days before numbers overwhelmed the defenders.
  • West: Indian troops contested every ridge. At Rezang La, Charlie Company of 13 Kumaon, outnumbered and under heavy shelling, fought almost to the last man and stopped the PLA reaching Chushul airfield.

Aftermath

  • 21 Nov 1962: China declared a unilateral ceasefire. It was wary of US or Soviet intervention, and both were busy with the Cuban Missile Crisis.
  • No peace treaty. China kept Aksai Chin and pulled back to pre-war positions behind the McMahon Line.
  • The defeat ended the idealistic, non-aligned Nehruvian posture and triggered a large expansion and modernisation of the armed forces.
IAF

Transport only, strike barred

LiftStrike barred
  • Political leadership barred offensive air power. This is the most debated aspect of the war.
  • Role allowed: supply, logistics and transport. An-12s, C-47 Dakotas and Otters air-dropped supplies, ammunition and winter gear into narrow, unmapped valleys in bad weather.
  • Mi-4 and Bell helicopters flew at their service ceilings to evacuate thousands of casualties.
  • Why strike was barred: fear of Chinese bomber retaliation on cities such as Calcutta, and thin early-warning radar cover.
  • Hunters, Mysteres and Canberras were kept out of ground attack and interdiction.
  • The judgement: the restraint is widely seen as a historic strategic blunder. Analysts hold that the IAF had a qualitative and quantitative edge over the PLAAF in Tibet, and that strikes on logistics choke points, passes and artillery could have changed the tactical outcome.

Aircraft and weapons used

  • An-12
  • C-47 Dakota
  • Otter
  • Mi-4
  • Bell helicopters
  • Hunter (held back)
  • Mystere (held back)
  • Canberra (held back)

1965

Second Indo-Pakistani War

J&K, Punjab, Lahore and Sialkot sectors

OutcomeCeasefire on 23 Sept. Tashkent Declaration restores earlier positions.

Cause

  • Ayub Khan saw Indian weakness after 1962 and had new US arms, including Patton tanks and F-86 Sabres.
  • Pakistan tested Indian defences and international reactions in the Rann of Kutch in early 1965.
  • Operation Gibraltar (Aug 1965): 26,000 to 33,000 soldiers disguised as local Kashmiris crossed the Line of Control to spark a rebellion and take Srinagar.
  • Locals did not rise. They alerted the Indian authorities, and the infiltrators were isolated and neutralised.
  • Operation Grand Slam (1 Sept 1965): a regular-army armoured thrust at Akhnoor (Chhamb-Jaurian) aimed at the Chenab bridge, which carried the only supply and communication line to Kashmir.

Course

  • 6 Sept 1965: Prime Minister Shastri authorised crossing the International Border, opening a Punjab front. Pakistan had to pull troops and armour away from Grand Slam.
  • Among the largest tank battles since World War II.
  • Asal Uttar, 8–10 Sept: Pakistan's 1st Armoured Division (M47 and M48 Pattons) pushed on Khem Karan to take Amritsar and the Beas bridges. India's 4th Mountain Division and armour breached canals to bog the Pattons down and drew them into a horseshoe trap. Nearly 100 tanks were destroyed or captured: ‘Patton Nagar’.
  • Lahore sector: Indian infantry reached the outskirts of Lahore and took Burki and Dograi.
  • Sialkot sector: India's 1st Armoured Division fought a grinding attritional battle that ended at Chawinda.

Aftermath

  • By late September both sides were short of ammunition and under UN, US and Soviet pressure. The UN ceasefire took effect on 23 Sept 1965.
  • Tashkent Declaration, Jan 1966 (Soviet mediation; Shastri and Ayub Khan): return to positions held before 5 Aug 1965.
  • India gave up hard-won gains, most notably the Haji Pir Pass.
  • Neutral assessments give India the upper hand at ceasefire: more territory taken and heavier Pakistani armour losses. Pakistan publicly claimed a stalemate.
IAF

Fully unleashed under Arjan Singh

Strike
  • Air Chief Marshal Arjan Singh led an IAF that, unlike in 1962, was free to strike.
  • Akhnoor: within an hour of the Army's request, Vampires and Mysteres hit the Grand Slam armour. Early losses to anti-aircraft fire and interceptors were heavy, but the strikes destroyed tanks and vehicles and bought hours to reinforce.
  • Sabre Slayers: Pakistan flew supersonic F-104 Starfighters and F-86 Sabres with Sidewinder missiles. The IAF had the small, subsonic, gun-armed Folland Gnat. Its small radar signature and tight turn won close turning fights and downed numerous Sabres.
  • Counter-air: Canberras and Hunters struck PAF bases at Sargodha, Peshawar and Mauripur. Aircraft were destroyed on the ground, runways cratered and supply chains degraded.

Aircraft and weapons used

  • Vampire
  • Mystere
  • Folland Gnat
  • Canberra
  • Hunter

1967

Nathu La and Cho La

Sikkim, then an Indian protectorate

OutcomeIndian artillery dominates. PLA deterred.

Cause

  • After 1962, Beijing believed the Indian military lacked the will to resist the PLA.
  • India began fencing the Sikkim border at Nathu La with wire to mark the line.

Course

  • 11 Sept 1967: PLA political commissars argued with Indian officers over the fence, then PLA troops opened point-blank machine-gun fire on exposed Indian engineers.
  • The setting differed from 1962. Major General Sagat Singh and Eastern Army Commander Lieutenant General Sam Manekshaw led a well-supplied force with political backing to hit back hard.
  • Days of accurate Indian artillery fire destroyed PLA bunkers, observation posts and command centres on the ridges above the pass.
  • Cho La, 1 Oct 1967: Gurkhas and other infantry fought hand to hand with kukris and bayonets and repulsed the PLA.

Aftermath

  • About 80 Indian casualties against estimates of over 400 Chinese.
  • Broke the myth of PLA invincibility on the high frontier and secured the Siliguri Corridor (the “Chicken's Neck”).
  • The deterrent effect kept China neutral in the 1971 war.
IAF

On alert, never needed

Hold
  • Fighter squadrons were fuelled, armed and on the highest alert, ready to strike if the PLA took the fight into the air.
  • They were not used. Army artillery had already established dominance.
  • Presence alone deterred the PLA Air Force from intervening.

1971

Third Indo-Pakistani War

East Pakistan, the western front, and the sea

OutcomeDacca surrender, 93,000 prisoners, Bangladesh born.

Cause

  • East Pakistan was politically, culturally and economically shut out by the West Pakistani establishment.
  • The Awami League won the 1970 election in a landslide. The West Pakistani junta refused to hand over power.
  • Operation Searchlight (March 1971): a systematic genocide against Bengalis, intellectuals and minorities.
  • Over 10 million refugees entered India, creating an economic, demographic and security crisis.
  • India trained, armed and sheltered the Mukti Bahini resistance.
  • 3 Dec 1971: Pakistan began formal hostilities with Operation Chengiz Khan, pre-emptive PAF strikes on 11 Indian airbases in the west, modelled on Israel's Six-Day War strikes. They largely failed and India declared war.

Course

  • A tri-service, multi-front campaign.
  • East: the goal was a rapid capture of Dacca. Armour and infantry bypassed fortified border towns, crossed rivers and encircled Pakistan's Eastern Command, helped by Mukti Bahini intelligence.
  • Navy: a blockade in the Bay of Bengal, with INS Vikrant launching strikes on coastal targets.
  • West: an active defence to deny Pakistan bargaining chips. At Longewala a large Pakistani armoured thrust was repulsed. India took ground in the Shakargarh bulge and pushed into the Sindh desert.
  • At sea: Operations Trident and Python used Osa-class missile boats against Karachi port, destroyers and fuel reserves.

Aftermath

  • 16 Dec 1971: Lt Gen A.A.K. Niazi surrendered unconditionally to Lt Gen J.S. Aurora. About 93,000 soldiers and paramilitary personnel gave up, the largest surrender since World War II.
  • A 13-day war ended with Pakistan split and Bangladesh born.
  • Simla Agreement, July 1972 (Indira Gandhi, Zulfikar Ali Bhutto): the Kashmir ceasefire line became the Line of Control, and disputes go to bilateral talks only, with no third-party or UN role.
IAF

Air supremacy, the high point

StrikeLift
  • 1971 is treated as the peak of IAF operations.
  • East: the PAF's No. 14 Squadron at Tejgaon, Dacca, was destroyed in the first 48 hours. Runways were cratered and aircraft hit on the ground, so the Army moved in daylight with no air threat.
  • Tangail Airdrop: a full parachute battalion dropped behind the lines to take the Poongli Bridge and cut off Pakistani forces retreating to Dacca.
  • Meghna Heli-Bridge: Mi-4s flew troops, heavy equipment and artillery across the Meghna past destroyed bridges, speeding the collapse of Dacca's defences.
  • West: Hunters strafed the exposed armoured column at Longewala.
  • Param Vir Chakra: Flying Officer Nirmal Jit Singh Sekhon of No. 18 Squadron (“Flying Bullets”) is the IAF's first and only PVC recipient. On 14 Dec 1971 six PAF F-86 Sabres attacked Srinagar airbase. He scrambled a Gnat, lost contact with his leader and fought all six alone. He hit one Sabre and set another ablaze before his aircraft was struck and he was killed. He is credited with saving the airbase.

Aircraft and weapons used

  • Mi-4
  • Hunter
  • Folland Gnat
  • Transport aircraft (Tangail)
1965 against 1971
Feature1965 war1971 war
CauseOperation Gibraltar (Pakistani covert infiltration)Genocide in East Pakistan; pre-emptive PAF strikes
Main theatreWestern front (Punjab, J&K deserts)Eastern front (riverine terrain of Bangladesh)
OutcomeStalemate, return to status quo anteTotal Indian victory, creation of Bangladesh
IAF roleCounter-air, close air support (Gnats against Sabres)Air supremacy in the east, airborne assaults, anti-armour
TreatyTashkent DeclarationSimla Agreement

1984

Operation Meghdoot

Siachen Glacier, around 18,000 ft

OutcomeIndia holds the key passes on the Saltoro Ridge.

Cause

  • Siachen sits near 18,000 ft between the Saltoro Ridge and the Karakoram. The Simla Agreement left it vaguely undemarcated.
  • Late 1970s and early 1980s: Indian intelligence, helped by Colonel ‘Bull’ Kumar's mountaineering expeditions, found Pakistan encouraging foreign expeditions to strengthen its claim and preparing to occupy the glacier.

Course

  • 13 April 1984: a pre-emptive move to occupy the commanding heights of the Saltoro Ridge before Pakistani forces mobilised.
  • Indian troops secured the key passes and have dominated the glacier since.
IAF

Flying where aircraft should not

Lift
  • Success hinged on the IAF's skill at altitudes where human survival is difficult.
  • IL-76 and An-32 transports lifted large stores into Leh.
  • Chetak and Cheetah helicopters, far above their designed service ceilings, ferried troops onto narrow ice walls and ridges.
  • Decades of continuous air maintenance of the glacier is called an unparalleled logistical feat in global military aviation.

Aircraft and weapons used

  • IL-76
  • An-32
  • Chetak
  • Cheetah

1987

Operation Pawan

Sri Lanka, around Jaffna and Vavuniya

OutcomeA long IPKF campaign against the LTTE.

Cause

  • After the Indo-Sri Lanka Accord, the Indian Peace Keeping Force (IPKF) deployed to disarm the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) and enforce a ceasefire.

Course

  • The mission turned into a protracted campaign of urban and dense-jungle warfare against a highly motivated guerrilla force.
IAF

Airlift and gunship support

LiftStrike
  • Tactical airlift moved troops quickly across the island.
  • Mi-25 and Mi-8 gunships gave casualty evacuation and close support.
  • Rocket strikes hit entrenched LTTE positions in the urban areas of Jaffna and the jungles around Vavuniya.

Aircraft and weapons used

  • Mi-25
  • Mi-8

1988

Operation Cactus

Maldives, Malé and Hulhulé airfield

OutcomePresident rescued. Mercenaries captured at sea.

Cause

  • Nov 1988: heavily armed mercenaries from a Tamil secessionist group attempted a coup, seized Malé and threatened President Maumoon Abdul Gayoom.
  • India answered a distress call from the Maldivian government at once.

Course

  • Elements of the 50th Independent Parachute Brigade flew from Agra to Hulhulé airfield within hours.
  • The paratroopers secured the airfield, rescued the President and captured the fleeing mercenaries at sea.

Aftermath

  • It is read as proof of India's standing as a net security provider in the Indian Ocean Region.
IAF

Agra to the Maldives in hours

LiftHold
  • IL-76 heavy transports carried the paratroopers directly from Agra to Hulhulé.
  • Mirage 2000 fighters escorted them to deter outside interference.
  • It is regarded as a flawless rapid-response mission.

Aircraft and weapons used

  • IL-76
  • Mirage 2000

1999

Kargil War

Dras, Kargil and Batalik, about 160 km along the LoC

OutcomeIntruders evicted. LoC status quo restored.

Cause

  • Winter 1998–99: Pakistan's Northern Light Infantry, posing as mujahideen, infiltrated across the LoC and took high bunkers that Indian forces had left under the customary winter withdrawal.
  • The positions stretched about 160 km across Dras, Kargil and Batalik and overlooked National Highway 1A.
  • Aim: cut the link between Kashmir and Ladakh and force a military and diplomatic capitulation.
  • For India, a major intelligence failure, months after the Lahore Declaration on bilateral peace.

Course

  • Fought under a nuclear overhang. Both states had tested in 1998.
  • India's leadership imposed strict restraint: no crossing of the LoC under any circumstances.
  • Operation Vijay (the second of that name): uphill infantry assaults above 16,000 ft.
  • Concentrated artillery, notably Bofors FH-77B howitzers in direct-fire mode, supported assaults that retook peaks including Tololing and Tiger Hill.
  • Heavy casualties from near-vertical climbs, sub-zero cold and no cover against entrenched machine guns.

Aftermath

  • India's restraint left Pakistan diplomatically isolated.
  • Nawaz Sharif went to Washington seeking intervention. Bill Clinton refused and demanded unconditional Pakistani withdrawal behind the LoC.
  • By late July 1999 the remaining intruders were evicted and the status quo ante restored.
IAF

Operation Safed Sagar

StrikeHold
  • The air campaign changed the doctrine of high-altitude air warfare.
  • Early problems: altitude altered bomb trajectories and cut the accuracy of unguided bombs. Pakistani Stinger missiles brought down a Mi-17, a MiG-21 and a MiG-27 in the first days.
  • Adaptation: Mirage 2000s with Litening targeting pods dropped laser-guided bombs on small fortified bunkers on ridges, hitting command, control and logistics hubs at Tiger Hill and Muntho Dhalo.
  • Top cover: MiG-29s flew continuous combat air patrols, which kept the PAF out of the fight.
  • The precision strikes weakened the intruders' hold and helped the infantry win.

Aircraft and weapons used

  • Mirage 2000
  • Litening pod
  • Laser-guided bombs
  • MiG-29
  • Mi-17 (lost)
  • MiG-21 (lost)
  • MiG-27 (lost)

2019

Balakot Airstrike

Balakot, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan

OutcomeJeM training facility struck. A new norm for retaliation.

Cause

  • A suicide bombing at Pulwama by Pakistan-based Jaish-e-Mohammed (JeM) killed 40 CRPF personnel.
  • India dropped the decades-old doctrine of strategic restraint and chose to hit the terrorists at source inside Pakistan.
  • This was the first open crossing of the international border since 1971.

Effect

  • It broke Pakistan's habit of using its nuclear umbrella to sponsor cross-border terrorism with impunity.
  • It set a “new normal” for Indian retaliatory strikes.
IAF

Operation Bandar

Strike
  • 26 Feb 2019, early hours: a package of 12 Mirage 2000s crossed into Pakistani airspace.
  • Weapons: SPICE-2000 standoff glide bombs and Crystal Maze missiles.
  • Target: a JeM training facility on a hilltop at Balakot, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. India says it was obliterated.
  • Support: Su-30MKI fighters as a protective screen, Netra AEW&C aircraft and mid-air refuelers.
  • It is presented as proof of deep-penetration, network-centric precision strike.

Aircraft and weapons used

  • Mirage 2000
  • SPICE-2000
  • Crystal Maze
  • Su-30MKI
  • Netra AEW&C
  • Mid-air refuelers

2020

Eastern Ladakh Standoff

Line of Actual Control, Eastern Ladakh

OutcomeIndia takes the Kailash Range heights. Phased disengagement follows.

Cause

  • May 2020: the PLA built up troops and manoeuvred along the LAC in Eastern Ladakh.
  • Galwan, 15 June 2020: hand-to-hand fighting in the dark with clubs and wire-wrapped rocks. Twenty Indian soldiers, including Colonel B. Santosh Babu, were killed. PLA losses were heavy but officially undisclosed.

Course

  • Operation Snow Leopard, late Aug 2020: Indian troops, including the Special Frontier Force, pre-empted the PLA and occupied the Kailash Range heights, including Rezang La and Rechin La south of Pangong Tso.
  • That put the Chinese Moldo garrison within range of Indian heavy weapons and gave India leverage.

Aftermath

  • China was pushed to the negotiating table, followed by phased disengagements.
IAF

Airlift at scale, fighters overhead

LiftHold
  • The rapid build-up was possible because of IAF strategic airlift, in a network-centric warfare setting.
  • Airlift: C-17 Globemaster III and C-130J Super Hercules moved tens of thousands of troops, T-90 tanks and heavy artillery to Ladakh's high airstrips.
  • Helicopters: newly inducted AH-64 Apache attack helicopters and CH-47 Chinook heavy-lifters added anti-armour deterrence and sustainment.
  • Fighters: Rafale and Su-30MKI flew forward, with combat air patrols over the Himalayas under an integrated air defence umbrella to deter Chinese air activity.

Aircraft and weapons used

  • C-17 Globemaster III
  • C-130J Super Hercules
  • AH-64 Apache
  • CH-47 Chinook
  • Rafale
  • Su-30MKI

2025

Operation Sindoor

Terror camps in Pakistan and PoK, then Pakistani military targets

OutcomeIndia hit nine terror sites on 7 May and Pakistani air bases and command centres by 10 May. Pakistan's DGMO called his Indian counterpart, and firing stopped from 5 pm on 10 May 2025.

Shown as stated by the Government of India, the armed forces and the Air Chief.

Cause

  • 22 Apr 2025: terrorists attacked tourists at Baisaran, near Pahalgam in J&K, and killed 26 people. India held Pakistan-based groups responsible; The Resistance Front, a Lashkar-e-Taiba proxy, was named.
  • India put the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance, closed the Attari check post and cut diplomatic staff, then gave the armed forces freedom to choose the response.

Course

  • 7 May 2025, 01:05 to 01:30: the armed forces struck nine terror sites: four in Pakistan, including the Jaish-e-Mohammed headquarters at Bahawalpur and the Lashkar-e-Taiba headquarters at Muridke, and five in PoK, including Muzaffarabad and Kotli.
  • India called the strikes focused, measured and non-escalatory: no Pakistani military facility was targeted on 7 May. The DGMO later said more than 100 terrorists were killed.
  • 7 to 9 May: Pakistan sent drones and missiles at Indian military sites and cities along the border. India's integrated air defence grid stopped them, and Indian forces hit air defence radars and systems, including at Lahore.
  • 10 May: after further Pakistani attacks, India struck air bases and military sites across Pakistan. The IAF's 11 May briefing showed strikes at Pasrur, Chunian, Arifwala, Sargodha, Rahim Yar Khan, Chaklala, Sukkur, Bholari and Jacobabad.

Aftermath

  • 10 May 2025: Pakistan's DGMO called India's DGMO at 15:35, and both sides agreed to stop firing from 17:00. India said the understanding was reached directly between the two militaries.
  • The government said Operation Sindoor is only paused and set a new normal: any terror attack will be treated as an act of war.
  • Honours, Aug 2025: nine Vir Chakras to IAF aircrew and four Sarvottam Yudh Seva Medals to IAF Air Marshals.
  • First anniversary, 7 May 2026: the services said the operation is not over and repeated that nine terror sites were destroyed and eleven airfields damaged.
IAF

Precision strikes and a wall of air defence

StrikeHold
  • Opening strikes: the Defence Minister and the IAF say Rafales fired SCALP cruise missiles and HAMMER bombs, and Su-30MKIs fired BrahMos-A missiles at terror and military targets.
  • Air defence: the IAF's IACCS network tied together the S-400, MR-SAM, Akash, SPYDER and legacy guns and missiles such as the Pechora and OSA-AK, with Army air defence, to stop waves of drones and missiles.
  • Air Chief, 9 Aug 2025: the S-400 shot down five Pakistani fighters and one large aircraft, an ELINT or AEW&C type. The large aircraft was hit at about 300 km, which he called the largest recorded surface-to-air kill. He said half of an F-16 hangar at Jacobabad and an AEW&C hangar at Bholari were hit, command centres at Murid and Chaklala were struck, and runways at Sargodha and Rahim Yar Khan were damaged.
  • Counter-air, 10 May: Air Marshal A.K. Bharti, then Director General Air Operations, briefed that the IAF hit air bases, command and control centres and air defence systems across Pakistan.
  • The Air Chief's view: the forces had full freedom to plan and execute, and the S-400 was a game-changer.

Aircraft and weapons used

  • Rafale
  • SCALP
  • HAMMER
  • Su-30MKI
  • BrahMos-A
  • S-400
  • MR-SAM
  • Akash
  • SPYDER
  • Pechora
  • IACCS

Synthesis

What changed from 1947 to now

Strategic outlook, extended to 2025

Trajectory

  • 1947 and 1962: defensive and reactive, against a tribal invasion and a border war.
  • 1971: decisive offensive manoeuvre warfare.
  • Through 2020: high-tech precision strike, as at Balakot and in the high-altitude moves in Ladakh.
  • 2025: Operation Sindoor repeated the deep-strike pattern at larger scale, with strikes on Pakistani air bases and S-400 air defence in the same four days.

Ahead

  • Future operations lean on network-centric and non-contact warfare.
  • Tri-service jointness and technological superiority are essential.
  • Planning problem: a possible two-front conflict with nuclear-armed neighbours.
  • Pillar: aerospace power joined to rapid-response mechanised ground forces, backed by resilient logistics nodes.
IAF

How the IAF's role changed

  1. 1962Transport and supply only. Strike barred.
  2. 1965Air combat and counter-air. Gnats beat Sabres.
  3. 1971Air supremacy and airborne assaults.
  4. 1999Precision strike at altitude (Safed Sagar).
  5. 2019, 2025Deep strikes inside Pakistan (Bandar, Sindoor).
  • By Kargil and Balakot the IAF stands as an independent strategic arm of deterrence, able to shape political outcomes without a full-scale ground war.

Current state · 17 October 2026

Where It
Stands

2942

The numbers that matter today: squadron strength, what is on order, what is late, the budget and the year's main news.

As of 17 October 2026

29

Fighter squadron strength

Against 42 sanctioned

29 in service (Air Chief: "29 to 30")13 short

Why

  • Old types retired faster than new ones arrived: the last MiG-21s went on 26 Sep 2025.
  • Tejas Mk1A deliveries are about two years late.
  • More retirements ahead: three MiG-29 squadrons and the Jaguar fleet are due to go towards the end of the decade.

Fix

  • The Air Chief says the IAF needs to add at least two squadrons (36 to 40 jets) a year just to stop the decline.
  • Plan: Tejas Mk1A at about 20 a year, MRFA Rafales at about 12 a year after a contract, 12 more Su-30MKIs, then Tejas Mk2 and AMCA.
  • In his words: "We have less numbers, but we are not weak."

Sources

  • The Week: Air Chief press conference
  • SSBCrack: 29 squadrons

₹

Defence budget 2026 to 27

Presented 1 Feb 2026

HeadAmountChange
Ministry of Defence, total₹7,84,678 croreAbout 15% over 2025 to 26
Capital outlay, defence services₹2,19,306 croreUp 21.8%
Aircraft and aero engines (all services)₹63,734 croreUp 31%

There is no separate Air Force line in the budget; aircraft buying for all services sits under the aircraft and aero engines head. Indigenisation: the 97-jet Tejas Mk1A order has over 64% Indian content, and AMCA prototypes will be built by a private-sector partner for the first time.

12 months

The year in the IAF

Oct 2025 to Oct 2026

  1. 17 Oct 2025

    First Tejas Mk1A from HAL's new Nashik line flies before the Defence Minister.

  2. 12 Nov 2025

    Nyoma (Mudh) airfield in eastern Ladakh opens; the Air Chief lands in a C-130J.

  3. Nov to Dec 2025

    Operation Sagar Bandhu: IAF relief flights to Sri Lanka after Cyclone Ditwah.

  4. 1 Feb 2026

    Union Budget 2026 to 27: defence ₹7.85 lakh crore, about 15% up; capital outlay ₹2.19 lakh crore.

  5. 12 Feb 2026

    DAC clears 114 Rafales under MRFA.

  6. 12 May 2026

    First Indian-built C-295 rolls out at Vadodara.

  7. 31 May 2026

    Gen N.S. Raja Subramani becomes Chief of Defence Staff.

  8. Mid 2026

    Fourth S-400 squadron delivered (reported).

  9. 1 Jul 2026

    Air Marshal Ashutosh Dixit becomes Vice Chief.

  10. Jul to Aug 2026

    IAF Rafales fly at Pitch Black in Australia, then Udara Shakti in Malaysia.

  11. 18 Sep 2026

    HAL delivers the first HTT-40 trainers and the last Tejas Mk1 twin-seaters.

  12. 26 Sep to 12 Oct 2026

    Tarang Shakti 2026 at Jodhpur, with US F-35s among the visitors.

  13. 3 Oct 2026

    The Air Chief's last annual press conference: 29 to 30 squadrons, and the Mk1A delay 'will hurt'.

  14. 6 Oct 2026

    Air Marshal Ashutosh Dixit named the next Chief of the Air Staff.

  15. 8 Oct 2026

    94th Air Force Day at Hindan, theme 'Infallible, Impervious and Precise'.

  16. 13 Oct 2026

    Reports say 712 of the 2,850 Agniveervayu in the first batch were retained as regular airmen.

  17. 25 Oct 2026

    Air Force Day flypast planned at Varanasi.

  18. 31 Oct 2026

    Change of Chief: ACM A.P. Singh retires and Air Marshal Ashutosh Dixit takes over.
